projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Yuhas was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: In Mississippi and the reason was that my father was part of the 37th Division, which was activated October 19th, 1940 with the 112th Engineers. He was a master sergeant. And he went down to Camp Shelby and so the family followed him. I went down at the age of 15 and then joined the Army from there. I was inducted at Camp Shelby September 15th, 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I think everybody remembers the day, if they were alive at that time, where they were. The same as if, the Kennedy assassination. I would say everybody knew just where they were on that day. Yeah, I was -- I was in downtown Golfport, Mississippi. I was just returning from a movie at 3:00 in the afternoon when I saw the headline on the Golfport newspaper saying that the Japs had attacked Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I was angry. It was unexpected. I just didn't think that those people knew what they were doing. They were taking on a world power and we had perhaps a slanted version of what the Jap was like. That his eyesight was poor and that he was diminutive. That may have been true, but as fighters they were something else. They were extremely good fighters. I have worked with the prisoners of war in representing their claims with the American Legion in the Veterans Administration and I have come to hear some of their stories about the Japanese treatment of them as a prisoner of war and the same with the Germans and the Koreans and a couple of Vietnam veterans. The in-human treatment by the Orientals and the Germans.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were still probably in high school then when the war started?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything for the war effort in those couple of final years of high school before going in?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: In a sense, yeah. We then moved up to Hattiesburg and I finished school at Brooklyn High School in Brooklyn, Mississippi and I worked in the canteen. One of the canteens at Camp Shelby as a young boy. I dispensed beer and pop to the soldiers and then soon became one myself. Before that for a limited time I helped sell the New Orleans newspaper. I can't recall the name of the paper now. In the barracks of the Japanese Americans, who went over to Italy and honored themselves and the American public in the way that they fought against the Germans. I'm sure the Germans must have wondered, good heavens why are they all the way over here and they were our guys and they did a terrific job. They were the most honored group, I understand, of any in the United States Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I got to know them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was the 442nd?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: 442nd and 100.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And so did you enlist or were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I was drafted. I got out of school in June of '43 and then went in the Army in August of '43, although not officially inducted until the following month. So then I went from Camp Shelby where my father was a (warden) officer in the prisoner of war camp at Camp Shelby. He told me a story about one of the German soldiers more or less got lost. He didn't escape. He got lost in the woods on one of their work details and he found his way back to the highway. He wanted to hitchhike back. He didn't want -- he had no wish whatsoever to go back to Germany. He liked it. Contrary to the way they treated our guys, of course, their homeland was being invaded and that no doubt makes a difference in your logic.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did your dad remain in the Army?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, he even went into the Korean war. He was a 20 year man. My brother, John, was 20 year Air Force. He went in in '44 till '64. And he was the most influential noncom at Camp Rickenbacker, the Air Force base in Columbus. I heard that from another guy. John never told me that. And my two son-in-laws are 20 year Air Force men. One of them is a past commander of the 13th District American Legion. I'm very proud of him because it appears that the Legion is grooming him to be the State Commander in about two years. Very proud of him. He is more like a son than a son-in-law.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So your dad must have been in his 40's then, so I suppose he didn't have to go overseas, right?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: That's right. That's right. Yeah, he was -- well, he was 39 when they were activated and then he stayed all the way until 53. He was with the National Guard, the 112th Engineers. Then when they were activated he went down there and that's -- that's really where I got an education. The teachers in Mississippi were more instructive than what we had here in Cleveland. The girl here would put it on the board and say, now go home and get your homework done and bring it back. But in Golfport and in Brooklyn, they were more intense and focused on what I can teach you, almost on an individual basis and I learned the English language from Mississippi. I learned that you don't say I have went. You say I have gone. You use the participle instead of the tense. I learned from them and never did I hear one word from any kid down there about damn Yankee, not once.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Those kids were beautiful to me, three years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when you went into the Army you probably didn't have a major adjustment to dealing with people from elsewhere in the country, right?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Not greatly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because you had been elsewhere.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, I went from there to Camp Barclay where Donald O'Connor, who recently died was stationed. He was a good kid. He had foot trouble, because he was a dancer in the movies. And the other was Rita Hayworth's brother, Vernon Cansino. He promised to bring her from Hollywood, but he might have done that after I had left for Springfield, Missouri to get more medical training before going overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about your training, your basic training?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Well, I ate things that I had never eaten before. You get so hungry because for the first time you really worked. You are digging sod and you can almost feel your shoulders expanding, that you were growing healthier and stronger. And when it was time to eat, I ate green beans for the first time in my life. I could have eaten the tray probably, too. You get so hungry. Except for Springfield, Missouri where the food was not too good and definitely Battle Creek, Michigan where the presidential candidate Bob --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Dole?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: -- Dole, he was there at around the same time. The food there was pathetic. You could have got sick on it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned for a particular outfit at that point?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I can't recall being called by any name, but my father came to the camp at, in Texas, Camp Barclay. And, of course, he was a master sergeant. So all of a sudden when he left -- that was to check on me, see how I'm doing, but he made an impression on the officers there and they, [cough] excuse me. They made me march all of these noncommission officers to class every morning, hut, two, three, four, and I was a lowly private. I think that my dad's visit had something to do with that. It was kind of the captain's tribute to him to let the kid go ahead and bring them to class. I never forgot that. My father was the bravest man I ever knew. And I could tell you of the incident, but I don't think you had the time. Very brave.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The incident from?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: It concerned a black man who was struck by a car in front of our house in Golfport and then the car sped away, but my father who was raking leaves saw it. Now, the blacks didn't have much respect in 1940 and '41, so he was left there to die, which he did. My father got the name of the license plate and took it to Court as a master sergeant. He took on the State of Mississippi on behalf of a black man and that is the most courageous thing I have ever seen or heard of. I was 16, but I never forgot what my father did. He took them on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The state was defending this driver?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Well, he had -- the car that struck him had a defense lawyer and my father went nose to nose with him when the guy got surly and my dad was tough. I got the scars to prove it. He just went nose to nose with him. Don't threaten me. I saw it. Took him on. I never knew what happened, whether the guy was convicted or not, but he took them on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So back to your training. Anything else from your training that you recall that stands out?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Well, you meet all walks of life. You finally get to meet the guy from Texas. Wonderful kid named Roscoe and a kid from Pittsburgh named Kelly and these guys from New York, which were indeed strange in the way they talked and the stories they told about Joe Box, who stole a canoe from a department store, walked out of the store with it. But when he came back from the (orders) they picked him up. You remember stories about that and the slang that they had. They would never say hundred they would say hundred (ph) and you just loved all those guys and maybe the best part of all these memories is the thought that you were young. Now, I'm old. And you think back you were young. You could do so many things and you met so many great guys and not all of them came back and that's the bitter part. So then from Springfield I went to Camp Shanks, New York and then got in a 40 ship convoy and went to Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About when was that crossing? That was just after D-Day. We arrived in Liverpool, England. Home of the Beatles in July of '44 and then after a stay around Bath, England we were shipped overseas and I was fortunately assigned to General Patton. His Third Army was formed on August the 1st and I joined him on the 15th of August. And that is one of the great things that happened to me. If you are going to serve serve with somebody whose name means something. And in a nationwide poll two years ago, Patton was named the greatest military general in our history. Consider Washington, Pershing, Grant, MacArthur, Eisenhower, Bradley were all generals. Patton was number one by the American public. This was just two years ago, not my generation, by the nation. And so when somebody would say what outfit did you serve with, Bob, I would say Patton. That was enough. You didn't say Company C Fifth medical battalion, whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was your job, were you a medic?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yes. I was a litter barrier with the Fifth Division and we treated cases. The first, I never will forget the first one. He was a tanker. To me they were the toughest guys in the Army, the tankers. He had -- his tank was on fire and the men were coming out of the tank and I'm just green. I'm brand new. I'm looking at my first combat and they are coming toward me and they bring the captain out of the tank. He had his leg blown off and we put a tourniquet on it. And his stump was smoking and he said that's like hanging a man. After he said straighten out my leg. And he looked to be a very handsome man, but he was burned and I wondered afterward. But the other tankers that we treated with a salve on their burns, they would lift their hands up in the air so that their hands wouldn't touch their body, their arms and never a whimper. They took it. And I thought, boy, this -- this is an idea of what the American soldier is like, Germany you asked for it. I mean they were two great fighters, great, great fighters.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was that the first action in France?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yes, France, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The fall of 1944?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, that was in August of '44, August 15th or 16th, first day. And the guy that assigned me to Patton was a guy who had served with my father and he asked me if John was my father. I said, yes. Momcamp was his name. And so he said, well, I'll take care of you and he did. I was wounded twice. But so were a lot of other guys. So were a lot of others that never came back. But I think he took care of me definitely.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me about the times you were wounded.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: It was a shell burst on September 20th, 1944 at Metz.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: city which was ringed by 22 forts and had never been taken by a frontal assault until Patton got there. It took us until the beginning of the Bulge to get the Germans out of there. Because they had tunnels inside the forts. They had automobiles, electricity, everything inside the forts. And so I happened to be outside and a shell burst. And I just felt something warm and wet on my leg and I froze at first, then backed into the shell -- into the fox hole and the other medic said, You have been hit, Bob. I said, Oh, I thought there was something wrong. He said, You are going to go back because you can get infection from that. So I went back for a month and then came back to combat. And then that's when the Battle of the Bulge. I was nearly killed. I should have been killed. I should have been killed. And that's another great story. But I made it until March 14th at Bitburg where President Reagan laid the wreath on the German grave. God bless him for that. Another shell hit behind me and I must have lowered my head instinctively and put my hands up because it tore a hole in my hand, my left hand and took my thumb off. And I have had fun with it. I have everybody doing thumbs up. When they don't have a thumb they invert it and high fours. So I have school kids doing that and all over the Federal building they do it. My family does it. I have had fun with it. You might as well. It is better to laugh than to cry. I think laughing is what is going to make you live longer. Look at Hope and Burns and Berl. I think you got to -- kind of got to find humor in it. I think the only thing a person can't find humor in is weather. There is nothing funny about snow or wind. Nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So tell me about the time that you were nearly killed.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: That was -- that was during the Battle of the Bulge. And we were up front and there was a huge man out in the field. He obviously was hit or dead and we're back a little ways, maybe a hundred yards from the body and on our right is a German machine gun, which had command of the field. In other words, if we were to go to that human being we had to be under the direct fire of that machine gun. And a Lieutenant, I like to think his name was Fox or maybe he was from Fox company. He said, I want a volunteer to go out and see if that man is alive. In looking right at me. They always told me don't ever volunteer. Oh, I'll go with you. That brave lieutenant took his helmet off. Although I had red crosses on both arms and four of them on my helmet to indicate to the Germans I'm unarmed. I'm a medic. I have no gun. I'm just going out to see if he's alive. And this Lieutenant bareheaded is going out with me as a further protection. And so Lieutenant says, We'll crawl halfway and then get up and run. And he took the side of the machine gun, too. But I think I was lagging a little bit behind him because I could see puffs of snow at my feet and I knew they were bullets that close. Now, afterward -- well, after we got back, I found out that from a pulse, there was no pulse. He was dead. The Lieutenant said, Do the same thing. We'll go back and thanks. And then I went back to where we were and I met a Vincent Sheaman, who was second only to Ernie Pyle as the correspondent. And I was shaking. It was about six below and we slept in that stuff. And I was 19 years old. He said to me, What is the matter son? Are you -- are you cold? I said, Yes, sir. The cold was only half of it. The other half was incredible fear that I had come that close to losing my life. Well, they took the machine gunners lined them up in front of the CP. And I had a chance to look at ten men that I thought at that time were trying to take my life. And I heard the Colonel give a command that meant they were not coming back. They were bleeding, but they still had the scowl like give me that machine gun and I'll do better the second time. But just a couple of years ago I'm sitting here in the house. When you have a lot of time to think as a widower and I'm thinking, you know something, maybe that German machine gunner could have killed me. All he had to do was raise his sights. But maybe in a moment of compassion he said, I'm not going to kill them. He is a medic, but I'm going to scare the hell out of him and the Lieutenant is going out there without a helmet. That would be the cowardly -- that's what I like to think, so. So since then I have included that German machine gunner in my prayers. Because I don't know. I'll never know. But I like to give it the benefit of the doubt. Maybe he could have, but didn't. And if you are good enough that you can put those bullets at my feet then all you have to do is lift it. I'm absolutely convinced of that and I hope that I'm right, that he would not have taken my life.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you say those machine gunners, how many of them were there?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: There were ten.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You said they were captured and then executed?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, they were executed. And so then a little while later I was wounded the second time in the hands and that was the end of the war for me. The infantry took us to the aid station and there was more shelling going on in the village than there was up where I was. And that was it. So then came a series of operations and I encountered the most heroic military man in the history of this country. Absolutely. His name was Red Erwin. I don't know if you have ever encountered him. He was Air Force and I want to put this on record. He seems to have been overlooked. He was in the hospital in Tuscaloosa, Alabama with me and 1,999 other guys. He was on a routine bombing raid somewhere in the Pacific. And they were ready to drop a phos shell, which is many thousand degrees, I would imagine. When it strikes the ground it sprays metal all over and it is hot metal. It sticks to the skin. You can't pull it out. It won't come out. It sticks. So you burn up from these hot pieces of shell fragments. And it failed to go through the bombay door. Threw it back into the plane and filled the plane with smoke. Somebody among those ten men had to pickup a white hot bomb, knowing the rest of your life is going to be, if you make it, to save the other nine. And Erwin chose to do it. He picked it up and began staggering to the pilot's window while the plane was lurching back and forth because of the weight of the bomb. He got to the pilot's window, but before he got to the pilot's window his hand struck the navigator's wooden table and his entire palm of his hand was imbedded in that wood. And then he staggered to the pilot's window and said, Excuse me, sir. And my brother said, No, he didn't Bob. I said, Yes, he did John. He was from Birmingham and that's the way they raised boys in the south. You know that. You know he said that. And he threw the bomb out the window and then collapsed breathing smoke. So they put him -- the plane returned and the Colonel found out and he sent a plane. He said, You get to Hawaii. There is a Medal of Honor in a glass case. Get it. Break the case if you have to. Bring it back here and I'm going to pin it on his chest before he dies. But he didn't die. He got the Medal of Honor quicker than any man in history. And he would walk around the hospital and he was such an inspiration to every one of us that would see his horribly disfigured shape and yet he walked naturally. That it minimized everything that we ever had wrong with us. If it was a leg off, an arm off, it didn't matter. Look at Red Erwin what he did for nine other guys. If I were one of those nine other guys I would be on the phone at least once a week, how are you doing, Red? Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. And so as long as I was there he was there and so when you got home you just didn't even think about anything being wrong with you. You just went on with a normal life and that's the way it has been for almost 60 years. I just don't believe this is anything. I think it is -- I think it has been a big help. I have had fun with it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How big was the phosphorus bomb, these were relatively small I assume, right?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: The what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The phosphorus bombs?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: See, I don't know. I wasn't in the Air Force. He picked it up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He obviously, I don't know, less than 100 pounds or something.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: It might have been.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think it was, if I remember.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: You know what, I never thought what you just said, but you have to be right because he picked it up and how many pounds can you pickup. That is true. I never thought of it that way. His entire was, what is that convex or concave. It was curved in. His entire side was just burned away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I think I know what you are talking about. It is like they drop all these sticks out of the bomber.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, I imagine it was small.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I have no idea what they weigh, but obviously it couldn't be a really big bomb.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: That's true. I never thought of it. That's true. I mean there is so many pounds you can pickup.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: But it was hot. It was red, white hot. And he did it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That detonated or going off inside.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, the bombay door failed to open. That's what happened at the back end of the plane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, gees.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: So I called him. One of the school kids said, Did you ever call him? I said, Yes, I did. One time about maybe 15, 20 years ago. Red, you don't know me. I was one of the guys in the hospital in Alabama that would see you walking the corridors. I want you to know -- he was a VA employee in Birmingham. I want you to know that you were an inspiration to all of us and all of us came home with a feeling of minimizing our disability, if you want to call them that, because of you. You are responsible for us getting through and Red simply said, Thank you. It was nice of you to call and that was it. He hung up. Maybe he was crying. I don't know. Maybe he -- he, I don't know. Maybe he didn't get many calls from those guys. I don't know what happened. But he didn't want to talk about it. But I owe a lot to that man.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was your outfit during the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Where was I at?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was your outfit in the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: In Sarlat-La. We were in the middle part of France. We were in Germany when the news came today. Today was the first day, December 16th, this day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 59 years.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: 59 years ago. That's right. The news came. Patton got the word that we got to go 100 miles north through ice and snow, sleet and rain and whatever and plug that gap. And so we pulled out of what appeared to be a sunny climate in Sarlat-La and head north in open trucks in freezing weather. And that's what happened. We got through Luxembourg, country that I didn't even know existed. You knew of the main countries, Belgium. We had heard about or heard later about the heroic stand of the 101st Airborne at Bastogne. God love them. They numbered ten to one and I met a guy who won the Medal of Honor in the Vietnam War. I worked with him. He was in 101st. I told him I have enormous respect for you, kid. That you would be in an outfit that has such a history. The tankers and airborne and the infantry, I love the infantry, but the tankers just seemed to be so doggone tough, just so tough. They just didn't let anything rattle them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I found out in my own way that it was best not to get too close to the guys that you served with or it can backfire on you. I think an officer might have really loved some of the men in his group, but he couldn't show it because if something happened to them, then he gave the order that might have caused their death or he might have just thought, oh, I really liked that kid. Now, I have got to write the letter to his parents or whatever the reason. You don't want to get too close to guys that you serve with. So I was never really close. I remember the ambulance backing up to the aid station and I saw two shoes on a litter, the bottoms of the shoes. They pulled the litter out and it was our staff sergeant in our group who had no right to go out. He was just going for supplies I guess and he saw a soldier in the field, lying in the field, and he jumped out of the truck and ran right across a land mine and a piece pierced his brain through the back of the head. A single piece of metal hit him in the exact spot that would have killed him and it did. And so to see him lying there, that was the first instant of someone that you were close to, as close as you wanted to get. You just didn't want to get too close. But you get friendships. Cline from Pittsburgh and Mauldin, Howard from Wisconsin. They were special. Boy, they were special.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything with those guys when you got a break from the action, anything for entertainment or to pass the time?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: No, not until -- well, I got -- I won the raffle. After the Battle of the Bulge ended on January 25th, Patton said, Give them passes to Paris. Take five names out of a helmet. Well, mine was one of the five. Can I go on? I'm in Paris now. You know what is going to happen. I was like a lot of kids. We had -- we didn't know the difference between a male and a woman. I had no idea. I knew that they made me feel funny and I felt very strange and I knew I wanted to do something, but I didn't know what to do. And we got to Paris, but before we got to Paris there were five of us whose names were picked out of a helmet. We stopped at a school house that became the surrender point of the German Army on May 8th or 7th, whenever date that was in '45, in that same school house they surrendered. Jodl signed his name. So the next day we get to Paris and fortunately, I was with a guy that I think he invented women. He knew so much about them. There was no question. There was the most incredible woman I have ever seen yet to this day. She was just a beautiful woman. And she was being solicited by an Air Force guy with the white scarf and everything and looked like Errol Flynn. Oh, come on Jerry, you can't make out with that. Watch me. You want her, Bob, you got her. And he did. He just talked her into going with me and he went with another one and she was my teacher. My love interest for three days. That's where I learned through her and she couldn't speak English and I couldn't speak French, but we spoke the language of the bedroom and got along great. She wanted to know if I was going to come back through Paris. That she would be in this bar and she would want to come back with me. I wonder how many German soldiers maybe, maybe, she said that, too. But I told her I don't think I'm coming back. That was in January and it was pretty close at that. I never have forgotten her. She was a model. She was a model in Paris. So you know that she was special. But that's where I learned at the age of 19. I think now they can learn almost at 19 months. Gee, what television doesn't pull any punches. They go all the way. There is nothing where you are trying to imagine when the curtain is closed in the movie in the 1940's what is going on back there. Then you finally find out what is going on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your outfit get any entertainment in the U.S. O shows or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, you know, the -- while the five of us were going to Paris the rest of them were being entertained by Marlene Detrick. God love her. She was wanted by Hitler. Hitler wanted her because she was German. She was entertaining our troops along the river and on the other side was the German Army. She was that close, that fearless. And so I missed her because I was in Paris. She was a wonderful, wonderful woman. And Bob Hope I think seemed to do most of his entertaining in the Pacific and those guys deserved it. I think if I -- how many times I reminded myself thank God I was in the European war rather than against the Japanese. They would not surrender. They would not surrender. And while they were both great fighters, the Germans and the Japs, the Germans did have some humanity.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call, getting letters?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Oh, boy, thanks. That's a good point. Yeah, we all looked forward to that and today when I meet some of these college kids and they are going to college. I tell them I'm going to write to you honey because I know what it meant to me to get mail. I had a girl, Helen, and she would write to me and then when I got home I found out she had married a sailor and he committed a form of suicide later on. So the girl that I met because I didn't stay with Helen or she didn't stay with me was the best thing that ever happened to me. My wife Frankie Hamlin was the greatest thing that ever happened. I told her you could have done so much better with someone else and she would keep saying, oh, no. Oh, no. And I would say, oh, yes. Oh, yes. She was an incredible and she was so pretty. Such a pretty little girl and I was so fortunate. We married when we were 24 years old and she had a stroke and left me on Christmas day '79. So this year will be 24 years. But she left me seven kids and they are all good. I tell them now don't call me. If your mother had survived you would be calling her every day, but don't call me. I know you love me. And call me if you need anything and don't use the word loan. It is not a loan. I'm able to give you something more now than I did when I was working and didn't make enough money. So anything you need you got. She was just wonderful.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Getting back to those letters from Helen, what kind of things would she write to you when Helen wrote?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I don't even recall. Probably the usual stuff that they write today, but I think love has lost its meaning.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And I told that to Linda. I said, Honey, I get these cards from some of the other kids that are now in school and they sign it love. But I told Lynn that I think maybe if you like a person it would mean more than if you love them because I think love has lost its meaning. You put love on cards and you wonder, well, it is just something that I have to say. It is obligatory, but it doesn't have the meaning that it did like when I would tell my wife and I would leave notes on the table I love you. That -- that was love. And I just wonder whether it has the same meaning today with the divorce rates and such that you read about and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you wrote to her were you able to tell her much about what you were doing?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah. No. We censored. Our mail was censored. So I didn't write too much about the war. No. I hinted to my father in a letter. Dad, I went over to Europe on the same ship that you came home on in World War I. So then after the war when we got together he said I caught that. You are talking about the George Washington. The ship that we captured from the Germans and we transported troops overseas. He came home on that. So did Woodrow Wilson in 1919. I guess they didn't trust the airplane then. Wilson had to come home on a boat, yeah. So I don't remember too much --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Only the operations and there was one visitation. Dennis Morgan visited us at the hospital in Alabama. He was the only celebrity I met head-on that I can recall. But I did meet after the war in this house a man who won the academy award and he, too, is a man that inspired me. He -- his hands were blown off. Harold Russell, [tape ended] he was National Commander of Amvets and the Amvets kid was sick. So I had to take Harold around the hospital, which is now Community College. It was then Criel Army Hospital. And so I asked Harold if he would mind stopping for a few minutes before he went downtown to appear on a TV show. Sure. And my wife met him and the two kids came tearing on recess. They came tearing home and met him and that was a high spot to have met him. He would take cigarettes out of his pack and everybody would hold their breath in the VFW. I took him down to the VFW convention the next day and he appeared there. And he would strike a match and again, everybody would hold their breath until he did it. And then they would rest. He can do all these things with two hooks and he lived with those hooks 60 years. Think about that. 60 years with hooks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And it is bad enough to think of someone with only one arm, but two hooks. He was such a great guy. He always had a wonderful disposition and the Amvets had the common sense to elect him four times as National Commander. He was a great figurehead for them. It was such a pleasure to meet him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: No, that's -- that's about it. I have no regrets, Tom, about having served. I have my own viewpoint on whether every kid should be given basic training of some kind, at least the year, as Bush does about Saddam. You know, he has his own personal feelings, but he is not expressing them. If he did he would probably be censored. Well, I have feelings. Thank God I served. I have something to carry with me to my grave and having worked in a hospital I remember sometimes even if the soldier had a family that he could be extremely proud of their accomplishments, his last thought was of the military. And I'm sure MacArthur in his speech to West Point, his last thoughts were of the -- what did he call it, of the Point, of the Point, of the Point. And that's -- that's the way I'll be and the way my two brothers who served and we just -- we just don't talk about it unless asked. And you have been very nice, Tom. You have been a credit to whatever you do. You sure made it easy for me to express my thoughts. I had no idea what I was going to talk about. The kids when I went to the school they didn't have any idea what the Purple Heart was. Some of them and I told them now you only get one Purple Heart. I have the medals. They are downstairs. Now, this little pin in the middle of it means it is a second wound. They don't give you two hearts. You get what they call an oak leaf cluster to the Purple Heart and the kids sent me something that I have in the albums. Their thanks. Each one of them had a word of thanks, 4th grade, 11th grade, 8th grade. They have all been very attentive. They don't move and I thought sometimes, very little hope sometimes I think for these kids, but when you get to talk to them and you see how riveted they are on you and the teacher says, I want you next year. He called me two days ago. He said, I want you back next year. And I speak to various groups, Tom. I speak to my own Division at their reunions. My Fifth Medical Battalion. I was a private and I'm talking to my former Colonels and Sergeants because they think I'm equipped to know how to make a speech. So for 12 years I have been doing that. Detroit, St. Louis, Dayton, wherever, wherever they have their reunions, mainly Toledo lately. And prisoner of war groups. They made me an honorary member. I'm just overcome with that. Because of the work I did for them as a service officer with the American Legion. I helped them get their 100 percent ratings based on full disability and I get free banquet dinners and I spoke twice at the National Cemetery in Medina on my wife's birthday, April 9th, which is POW-MIA day and then at the, where they break the ground, groundbreaking.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I spoke there with Congressman Tom Sawyer and the other guy was such a doll. He is from Lorain. I can't think of his name. Wonderful guy. [tape ended.] There was one --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is all part of it.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: -- one incident where I did take three prisoners for heaven sake when I think about that. I find myself sometimes walking by myself. I don't know how this happened, Tom. I don't know why. I found myself alone on so many interludes. And I'm approaching the top of the mountain where I could look down the mountain. All of a sudden three German figures come up over the top of the mountain and they are approaching me and I'm so cold that your brain is numb. You don't even think Tom, what is happening here. If they are going to kill you maybe you would almost welcome it. But they put their hands behind their heads, which is a signal that they are surrendering to me, a medic. And so I told them to just go on back and to that extent I captured three Germans. Then I went a little bit farther and there was a shrubbery here like you see in yards and I stepped between two bushes and here is an American soldier lying on his back with a scowl on his face and he is frozen in the position that he had been firing his machine gun. The gun is pointed toward the sky and he is dead, but he is ringed by a half a dozen German soldiers that he took with him before they got him. I never forgot that. What a heroic guy that was and whether whoever came upon him recognized what he had done just as I did. Here are the dead German soldiers and here he is. Boy, there is some things that linger with you. Heroic, and oh, this is the other point. When people say that all heroes and Audie Murphy said it. I don't think he realized what he said. But all heroes are dead heroes doesn't know what he is talking about. Your father was one. Anybody who was a prisoner of war was a hero. So many -- Audie Murphy was a hero. Red Erwin was a hero. Some would say, Well, he was fool hearty. Yeah, but he saved the lives of nine other men. Isn't that what they tell you about in the Bible? That you give your life for someone else. It is in the Bible. Well, indeed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As a medic you never carried a weapon; is that right?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Right, and thank God for that, Tom. I had no idea how to shoot a gun. I, whew, I don't know. I'm glad I didn't carry a gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So those Germans that surrendered to you must have known you didn't have a gun, they just wanted to give up?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, they wanted to give up. We did capture a German medic and he appeared to help us on our litter squad. He took one of the handles when we picked up some of the wounded and he was happy. He was so elated that he was now a part of the American Army and he is going to the rear. He is out of this thing. He was a beautiful kid. What a war. I'm so glad it happened to me. I'm so glad. Oh, what a blessing that thing was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I can see why you speak. You are inspirational.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Aw.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: No, I can't think of anything, Tom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How did you get your, earn your Bronze Star?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Well, that was where I went out with the Lieutenant. He must have reported it, but I went out there and was subjected to fire. I hope he got something out of that, too. Yeah, that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And the Nazi flag, where did you get that?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: My brother picked that up at an auction.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And he said, Bob, I got something for you. I think the guy said this was flown over Berlin. It looks big enough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: [tape ended.] The fourth armored, that was Patton's favorite and they were the tough guys. Now, when I went back and was hospitalized the first time I met some of them and they wanted to get back. They are in bandages and they want to get back. I thought, man, no wonder Patton loves these guys. They are the toughest. They were the equivalent of the Marines any time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And I love the Marines. Tom, I know a kid he was my boyhood friend, Eddie Krejci, K-r-e-j-c-i. He got his father to get permission to join the Marines at age 15.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: At age 16 he was bayoneted by the Japs on Guam. They said they could hear his screams all over the island. One month shy of his 17th birthday. I look at some of these kids that seem to be just wasting their lives. You don't know what to do with your life then join the military. It is great. You will have a great experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And look what those kids did over there. They captured that rat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, that was a surprise.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Oh, boy, that was such good news. My daughter called me and told me and then the way he looked.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I know it.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Ewee, [tape ended.] There is no partitions and you are sitting there and you are doing your job. You are 18, 19 years old. You don't care. It doesn't matter. Now, it matters. And you go to the urinal. We weren't prepared for war. So everything was make-shift, you know. And when you get overseas, well, what did you do. You dug a trench about this wide and you dug a trench and you straddled it and you did your job. And you did, well, the other way, the urinary you can do anywhere, but you did it in the trench. Nobody ever asked that question. Well, what did you do when you had to go? I think that would be interesting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, we have got it. I left it running.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Oh, you left it running.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I got it.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Son of a gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I never really asked it. I heard a lot of latrine stories.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About latrines exploding. But I never heard anybody just talk about using the latrines.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I began to wonder, you know. When you are a widower you have got a lot of time to think. Now, that the kids are gone you have more time to think. I thought son of a gun, nobody ever asked that question. So I'm on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I know. That's right. So we got that. As far as I know that's the first one I have got. I sent in 160 of these.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Well, I think it is worthwhile.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly. Was that a tough adjustment? Well, I guess in training you had stalls probably, right?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you --

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Well, no, in training that's what it was, you would just get --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was a latrine, just dig holes in the plank or whatever.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, they were toilet bowls. But there was no partition. You could talk to a guy over here and over here while you were doing your job.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You just accepted that that was part of Army life.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, and cleanliness, you got to keep your shoes polished, which I have often wondered about and the love, Tom, the love we had for Mauldin.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Mauldin.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Gees, I can't think of his first name.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bill.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Bill Mauldin. His cartoons, beautiful views, one for the enlisted men. Two officers standing on a cliff with the rainbows and the genius of Mauldin. When he had a calvery sergeant pointing the gun at the hood of his jeep because the wheel broke. He was going to shoot it like he would the horse. The genius of Mauldin and now he is gone. And Ernie Pyle his stories.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: We had all that that other wars don't have. The greatest journalists, the greatest cartoonist.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: The greatest spirit. You knew why you were fighting. You knew it. You knew who the enemy was and you knew where he was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was some --

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Your father is a hero. Your father is a hero.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: See, they don't, some of those guys took a (platter) with that, just that way of thinking. I didn't do anything. I was a prisoner. Bologna. They took abuse. They lost their self-identification. They -- they are nothing to the Germans and certainly the Japanese because the Jap thought it was criminal that you would give up. Shame on you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly. In his case it was mostly they didn't have food for themselves so they certainly didn't have food to share with the prisoners.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, that's true, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There were two-thirds of the guys in his labor camp starved to death.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: You know what MacArthur liked to remind them. MacArthur liked to remind the Japanese only six percent of our armed forces is being used to beat you guys. Everybody else is in Europe

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: But those marines, oh, God love them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Tom, I'm going to tell you one story. I know you got other things to do. One time at work I'm filing a claim. It was a black guy and he's looking at the ground when he comes in and after a little while looking at the floor he said, I was at Iwo Jima. I thought, I have never seen a picture of a black in Iwo Jima. They all looked white to me. And I looked at his discharge. He was. He said, I want to tell you. You probably had your doubts. He said, We were bringing in the supplies on the beaches. There was a black kid standing next to me 19-years-old. He got a bullet right in the forehead standing right next to me. I was that close, but I was on Iwo Jima. I stood up. I told him, I'm honored. I shook his hand. I said, I'm honored to find somebody that survived Iwo Jima and there's one thing I tell them in my speeches. When you see a black man dying or being wounded on a battle field and nearby is a white man being wounded or dying on a battle field, the same field, you notice that the color of their blood is the same. The group is paralyzed. Nobody moves. I don't think it ever occurred to put it in that way. The color is red whether he is black or white. [tape ended] And all right, one more story of a black.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: One more. This is when I'm wounded now. My hands are crossed and the nurses are feeding me. The guy next to me is the only black guy on the ward. Oh, gees, what was his name. Well, Clifford, let's say Clifford. It wasn't, but it was close enough. And we got to talking when you are in a mood to talk and he had -- he had the wound in the hand. The Chaplain came to the head of the ward. This is a 40 bed ward. He is at the head of the ward. He said, Is there anybody that wants books or magazines? I'll bring them back. And he raises his hand. He was the only one. The only one. Get it. He is black. The only guy raising his hand. And the minister said, What is your name? He got it. And then he left. Ten minutes later, how could you forget the guy's name? He got to the head of the ward. He said, which one is Clifford? Now, if you don't learn something even at your, at the age of 19 you are pretty damn dumb if you don't understand what he is trying to teach you is humanity, fellowship, whatever the word you want to use. To me he looks like all the rest of you guys and he is making that point.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: See, a lot of things you can pickup in the war. I have no regrets. You got me in tears, Tom, when I recall some of this stuff. I'm so happy. I'm glad you stopped. [tape ended] There was a policeman that died recently, a year ago that I wish you had met. He was in the second wave of D-Day. A little cop, Maserella.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: He was in the second wave and he was a guy that kept encouraging me to make these speeches. He would say, Bob, I want you here. I want you there. And I made a speech in Lakewood Park with the mayor there. It was packed, on November 11th, last year. Six days later he died. He was there and then six days later he died. He was the -- now, he is a little cop. He was state president of the Fraternal Order of Police two years in a row. That -- see, the friends that you acquire in this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: How would I have met him otherwise? How would I have met Harold Rossover or these wonderful guys that you serve with. How could you have served with Patton? So many guys have said they saw that movie. My brother said I have seen it six times, Bob. And his wife says, yeah, I'm getting tired of looking at it. Tom --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I hope he owns it and doesn't rent it anymore.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Well, I guess he catches it on TV.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Inaudible)?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And he doesn't care what hour. He will watch it. He was with LeMay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And John told me that he was part World War II. He said they A bombed Cleveland three times.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Practice, practice.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And I told people that. I said, Does that make you feel good? Where was the air defense command? That was my other brother. And my brother that A bombed us would tell everybody he was on a coffee break while I was A bombing Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was ground zero turbo power.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: John also A bombed Pittsburgh three times.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And I said to John, Well, you probably wouldn't know the difference. My wife was from Pittsburgh so that's the only bad thing I would ever say about her.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were those cities the right size to compare to the potential targets in your band?

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, I guess so. I guess so. Plus, they were originating from Columbus. So it was a short trip.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Short trip, yeah, you are right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And so I said to my kid brother, Where the hell were you, Ron?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: So we have a lot of fun. Like I say, you can find fun, some laughs even in combat, but not the weather. There is nothing funny about a 100 mile an hour wind like they had in the Federal building that day. Nothing funny about that. People being thrown across the street and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The weather you had during the Bulge, too.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Yeah, see the kids find that hard to believe. Well, how did you sleep the kid asked me. I said, You dug a hole. You better dig a hole because Patton would demand it. And you didn't go into the towns because he knew they would shell the towns. You dug a hole and got into the hole. Pulled your overcoat over you and you slept and the reason you could do it was because you were 18 and 19 years old and you can't do it now, of course, or even maybe in your 20's, but that's how. You're young and that is probably maybe the happiest thought of the war. You were young and look what you did. Look what you accomplished --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: -- with all these wonderful guys. So much heroism. You saw it all over, Tom, all over. And some would say it died and they are all buried. We went, our guys had a reunion and they decided to go to Europe when the terrorists were really active. So 23 of us went over back there for three weeks and we saw the cemetery above Omaha Beach.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Where the crosses are upright in perfect alignment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: I can't believe how they did that. All the same height and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: -- if you can't cry in that cemetery. It was in Saving Private Ryan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: That cemetery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And then farther up the one where Patton is buried in Luxembourg, where but for the grace of God I would be buried, 5,000 more there. And they put him in with the other guys, Tom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: His was just a cross among all these GI's.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: And the people were trampling over all these graves to get to him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: All right already, let's dig him up and put him at the head of the column. So graves go like this pointing toward his stone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: Under a low wall. General Patton, the same statistics that the private had, very simple, George S. Patton General, whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Yuhas
sp.p: That's the way he would have liked it and I think he died because God decided to take him home. There is no more war, George. Come on home. You are just going to louse up everything with that big mouth of yours and so come on home. And I know he would have wanted to die by a bullet, but. I'm just so proud of everything and you made me rehash it all. I'm so glad you did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I am, too. [Tape ended.]
